Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 3:

﴿We recite to you﴾ (نَقْرَأُ عَلَيْكَ), i.e., Jibril recites it by Our command. The object of "natlu" (natlū, "We recite") is ﴿from the news of Musa and Fir'awn﴾, i.e., We recite to you some of their account ﴿in truth﴾ (بِالحَقِّ). The phrase is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), i.e., while they are truthful (muḥiqqīn). ﴿For a people who believe﴾ (لِقَوْمٍ يُؤْمِنُونَ), i.e., for those whom We know in advance will be believers, because the recitation benefits only these people and not others.

Indeed, Pharaoh (Fir'awn) is a resumptive sentence (jumla musta'nafa) serving as an explanation of the preceding sentences, as if someone had asked, "And how was their story?" So he said: Indeed, Pharaoh ﴿exalted himself﴾, transgressed and went beyond all bounds in oppression, became arrogant, boasted of himself, and forgot servitude ﴿in the land﴾, that is, the land of his kingdom, meaning Egypt. ﴿And he made its people into factions (shiya')﴾, groups that follow him in what he wishes and obey him, so that none of them could turn his neck (away from him); or, groups differing from one another, honoring one group and humiliating another, so he honored the Copts and humiliated the Israelites. ﴿Subjugating a group of them﴾, namely the Children of Israel, ﴿slaughtering their sons and keeping their women alive﴾, that is, leaving the girls alive for service. (p-628) The reason for slaying the sons was that a soothsayer (kahin) told him: "A boy will be born among the Children of Israel through whose hand your kingdom will be taken away." This is evidence of the folly of Pharaoh, for if he believed the soothsayer, killing would not benefit him, and if he disbelieved him, then what is the point of killing? As for "yastad'if" (subjugating): it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "ja'ala" (made), or an attributive (sifa) for "shiya'an," or an independent statement (kalam musta'naf). And "yudhabbihu" (slaughtering) is a substitute (badal) for "yastad'if." ﴿Indeed, he was among the corrupters﴾, that is, the killing of the innocent is indeed the act of corrupters, since it has no benefit whatsoever, whether the soothsayer spoke truly or lied.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 5:

﴿And We wish to bestow favour﴾ — natafaddalu (We bestow grace). This is a proof for us in the question of al-aslah (what is most beneficial for the servant; the doctrine that God necessarily does what is best). This clause is conjoined (ma'tufah) to ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 4], because it is similar to that clause in its occurrence as an explanation (tafsir) of the account (naba') of Musa and Pharaoh, and as a narrative relating it (iqtisas laha); or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from yastad'if (he oppresses), meaning: Pharaoh oppresses them, while We wish to bestow favour upon them. The will of God the Exalted is an existent reality, so it is treated as if it were concurrent with their oppression. ﴿over those who were oppressed in the land and make them imams﴾ — qadah (leaders) who are followed in good, or leaders toward good, or governors (wulah) and kings (muluk). ﴿and make them the inheritors﴾ — i.e., they inherit Pharaoh and his people's kingship and everything that belonged to them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 6:

﴿And We would establish﴾ — makkana lahu means that he made a place for him on which he might sit or lie down. The meaning of establishing (al-tamkin) ﴿for them in the land﴾ — that is, the land of Egypt and Syria — is that He makes it such that it does not reject them, empowers them, and executes their command. ﴿And We would show Pharaoh and Haman and their hosts﴾ — with a damma on the nun and a fatha on Pharaoh and what follows it, and with a ya' and a raf' on Pharaoh and what follows it, read by ʿAlī and Ḥamzah. That is, they would see from them what they feared: the loss of their kingdom and their destruction at the hand of a boy born among them. Yurā (with the ya') with a fatha is in coordination (ʿaṭf) with the object preceding it, like the reading with the nun, or with a damma as a new sentence (istiʾnāf). ﴿from them﴾ — from the Children of Israel. It is connected to nurī and not to yaḥdharūn, because the relative clause (ṣilah) may not precede the relative pronoun (mawṣūl). ﴿what they were wary of﴾ — al-ḥadhar is taking precaution against harm.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 28, verse 7:

﴿And We inspired the mother of Moses﴾ by inspiration (*ilham*, a direct insight placed in the heart), or by a dream, or by the report of an angel, as it was for Mary. This was not the revelation of a messenger, and she was not a messenger. ﴿To suckle him﴾. The *an* here is in the sense of *ayy* (namely), or it is a verbal *an* (*masdariyyah*). ﴿And if you fear for him﴾ from being killed, namely that the neighbours would hear his voice and inform on him, ﴿then cast him into the river﴾, the sea. It is said that this is the Nile of Egypt. ﴿And do not fear﴾ drowning or being lost, ﴿and do not grieve﴾ at being parted from him. ﴿We shall surely return him to you﴾ by a gentle means, so that you may raise him, ﴿and make him one of the messengers﴾. In this verse there are two commands, two prohibitions, two reports and two glad tidings. The difference between fear (*khawf*) and grief (*huzn*) is that fear is distress that befalls a person over something expected, while grief is distress that befalls him over something that has happened, namely his separation from him and the anticipation of it. So she was forbidden from both, and given the glad tidings of his return to her and of his being made one of the messengers.

It is narrated that ninety thousand newborns were slaughtered in the search for Moses. It is also narrated that when her labour pains came upon her, one of the midwives who had been appointed over the pregnant women of the Children of Israel, and who was a friend of hers, attended to her. When he fell to the ground, a light between his eyes overwhelmed her, and love for him entered her heart. She said: "I have come to you only to kill your newborn and to inform Pharaoh. But I have found for your son a love the like of which I have never found. Keep him hidden." When the midwife left, Pharaoh's spies came, so she wrapped him in a cloth and placed him in a heated oven, and she did not know what she was doing, because her mind had been confused. They searched but found nothing, and they left, while she did not know where he was. Then she heard his crying from the oven, so she hurried to him, and God had made the fire cool and safe for him. When Pharaoh pressed hard in the search for the boy, God inspired her to cast him into the river, and so she cast him into the river after she had suckled him for three months.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 8:

﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up﴾ — akhadhahu (they took him). Al-Zajjaj said: Pharaoh was from the people of Fars, from Istakhr. ﴿So that he might become an enemy to them﴾ — i.e., so that the matter would end up in that outcome, not that they took him up for this purpose. It is like their saying: "For death is what the mother bears" — and she did not bear him so that her child would die, but the outcome was headed toward that. So said al-Zajjaj. On this basis the exegetes said that this is the lam of consequence and outcome (lam al-'aqibah wa al-sayrurah). The author of al-Kashshaf said: it is the lam of kay (lam kay), whose meaning is causation, as in your saying: "I came to you so that you would honor me." But the meaning of causation in it comes by way of metaphor, because when that was the result of their picking him up, it was likened to the motive for which the doer performs the act, namely honoring, which is the result of coming. ﴿And as a grief﴾ — wa-huznan: 'Ali and Hamzah read it as huzn, and they are two dialects, like 'adam and 'udm.

﴿Indeed, Pharaoh and Haman and their soldiers were sinners﴾ — "khati'in" is lightened to "khati'in" by Abu Ja'far, i.e., they were guilty. So God punished them by raising their enemy and the one who would be the cause of their destruction at their hands. They were sinners in everything, so their error in raising their enemy is not a novelty from them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on Surah 28, verse 9:

﴿And the wife of Pharaoh said: "A comfort of the eye for me and for you."﴾ It is related that when they picked up the chest, they tried to open it but could not. They then tried to break it, but they were unable to do so. Āsiyah approached and saw a light coming from inside the chest. She worked at it and opened it, and there was a child whose light was between his eyes. They loved him. Pharaoh had a daughter who was afflicted with leprosy (*baraṣā'*). She looked at the child's face and was healed. Then the wicked ones among his people said, "This is the one we fear from him. Permit us to kill him." Pharaoh was resolved to do so, but Āsiyah said, "A comfort of the eye for me and for you." Pharaoh said, "For you, but not for me."

In a hadith: "Had he said what she said, Allah the Exalted would have guided him as He guided her." This is stated as a hypothetical: that is, had he not been sealed upon his heart, like Āsiyah, he would have said the same thing as she said and would have become Muslim as she did.

"Qurratu" is the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*), meaning: "He is a comfort." "Lī wa-laka" are two descriptive phrases (*ṣifatān*) modifying "qurratu."

﴿Do not kill him.﴾ She addressed him in the manner of kings, or she addressed the wicked ones.

﴿Perhaps he will benefit us.﴾ For there are in him signs of good fortune and indications of benefit, because of what she witnessed of the light and the healing of the leprous girl.

﴿Or we may take him as a son.﴾ Or we may adopt him, for he is worthy of being a son to kings.

﴿While they do not perceive.﴾ This is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), and its referent (*dhū ḥāl*) is the family of Pharaoh. The sense of the sentence is: the family of Pharaoh picked him up so that he would be for them an enemy and a source of grief, and Pharaoh's wife said such-and-such, while they did not perceive that they were in a great error in picking him up, in hoping for benefit from him, and in adopting him.

As for His words ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh...﴾ (Qur'an 28:8), this is a parenthetical clause (*jumla i'tirāḍiyya*) placed between the conjoined element and that to which it is conjoined, emphasizing the meaning of their error.

How beautiful is the arrangement of this speech, according to the scholars of *ma'ānī* (the science of meaning) and *bayān* (the science of expression)!

(p-631)

And the heart of Moses' mother became empty (fārigan) — devoid of reason (ṣifran min al-ʿaql) — because of the overwhelming anguish that seized her when she heard that he had fallen into the hand of Pharaoh. ﴿Had she not been that she would have disclosed it﴾: the pronoun in "bihi" refers to Moses, and what is meant is his matter, his story, and that he was her son. It is said: when she saw the waves playing with the chest, she nearly cried out and said, "O my son!" It is also said: when she heard that Pharaoh had taken the chest, she did not doubt that he had killed him, so she nearly said, "O my son!" out of compassion for him. Inna (an) here is a lightened form of the heavy inna, meaning: she nearly (kādat). ﴿Had We not fortified her heart﴾: had it not been that We fortified (rabaṭnā) her heart — and "fortifying the heart" (al-rabt ʿalā al-qalb) means strengthening it by inspiring patience. ﴿So that she might be among the believers﴾: among those who affirm Our promise, which is that "We will return him to you." The answer to "law-lā" (had it not been) is omitted, meaning: she would have disclosed it. Or: (her heart was) empty of worry when she heard that Pharaoh had adopted him, so that she nearly disclosed that he was her son, because she could not control herself out of joy and delight at what she had heard — had We not calmed her heart and quieted her agitation, which arose from the intensity of joy, so that she might be among the believers, the ones who trust in God's promise and not in Pharaoh's adoption.

Yusuf ibn al-Husayn said: Moses' mother was commanded with two things, forbidden two things, and given two glad tidings, yet all of that did not benefit her until God Himself took charge of her protection, so He fortified her heart.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 11:

﴿And she said to his sister﴾, Maryam, ﴿"Follow him"﴾, meaning: follow his track, so that you may learn his news. ﴿And she watched him﴾, meaning: she saw him, ﴿from afar﴾, meaning: from a distance. It is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) referring either to the pronoun in *bihi* (the "him" in "watched him") or to the pronoun in *baṣurat* (the subject of "she watched"). ﴿While they did not perceive﴾ that she was his sister.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 12:

﴿And We had forbidden to him the wet-nurses﴾, a prohibition of prevention (tahrim man') and not a prohibition of the Law (tahrim shar'). That is: We prevented him from suckling at any breast other than his mother's. He would not accept the breast of any nurse, until this caused them concern. Al-marada' (the wet-nurses) is the plural of murdi' (a nursing woman), who is the woman who suckles; or it is the plural of marda' (a place of suckling), meaning the breast or the act of suckling. ﴿Before﴾ — before the tracing of his trail (qassihā atharahu) or before We returned him to his mother. ﴿Then his sister said﴾ — she had entered among the wet-nurses and saw that he would not accept a breast — ﴿Shall I direct you﴾ — I guide you — ﴿to a household who will take charge of him﴾, that is, Musa, ﴿for you, and they will be sincere to him﴾. Nush (sincerity) is the performing of an act free from any admixture of corruption. It is narrated that when she said "and they will be sincere to him", Haman said: "Indeed she knows him and knows his family, so seize her until she informs us about the story of this boy." She said: "I only meant: they will be sincere to the king." So she set off to her mother by their command and brought her, while the child was in the hand of Pharaoh, who was distracting him out of compassion for him, and he was crying, seeking suckling. When he smelled her scent, he became at ease and took her breast into his mouth. Pharaoh said to her: "Who are you to him? For he has refused every breast except yours." She said: "I am a woman of good scent and good milk; no child is brought to me but that he accepts me." So he handed him over to her and gave her a stipend, and she took him to her home. And God fulfilled His promise of return, and so it was established and settled in her knowledge that he would be a prophet; and that is His saying.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 13:

﴿So We returned him to his mother, that her eye might be cooled﴾ by staying with him ﴿and she would not grieve﴾ at his separation ﴿and that she might know that the promise of Allah is true﴾. That is: and that her knowledge might be confirmed by direct witnessing, just as she knew it by report. His saying "and she would not grieve" is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "that her eye might be cooled." As for the dinar that she was taking every day, as al-Suddi said, it was lawful for her because it was the property of a non-Muslim enemy (harbi), not because it was a wage for nursing her son. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ — this is included within her knowledge; that is: that she might know the promise of Allah is true, but most people do not know that it is true, so they doubt. It also resembles an allusion (ta'rid) to what had escaped from her when she heard the news of Musa and grew distraught.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 14:

﴿When he reached his maturity (ashuddah)﴾ Musa reached the peak of strength and the completion of intellect. Ashudd is the plural of shiddah, like ni'mah and an'um according to Sibawayh (the early grammarian, d. c. 180 AH, whose Kitab is the foundational work of Arabic grammar). ﴿And he attained full maturity (istawa)﴾: he became balanced and upright, and his firmness was complete. This was at forty years of age. It is related that no prophet was sent except at the age of forty.

﴿We gave him wisdom (hukman)﴾: prophethood. ﴿And knowledge (ilman)﴾: understanding of the law (fiqh), or knowledge of the interests of both abodes (this world and the Hereafter).

﴿Thus do We reward the good-doers﴾: that is, just as We did with Musa and his mother, We do with the believers. Al-Zajjaj said: God, exalted is He, made the granting of knowledge and wisdom a recompense for good conduct, because they lead to Paradise, which is the reward of the good-doers. And the knowledgeable wise person is the one who acts upon his knowledge, because He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And wretched is what they sold their souls for, if only they knew﴾ (2:102). So He made them ignorant, since they did not act upon knowledge.

﴿And he entered the city﴾, that is, Egypt, ﴿at a time of heedlessness of its people﴾. The phrase *ʿalā ḥīni ghaflatin* is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial clause, describing the state of the subject) of the agent of the verb, meaning he was concealed. This was the time between the two evening prayers (*al-ʿishāʾayn*), or the time of *al-qāʾilah*, meaning the middle of the day. It was also said that when he grew up and came of age, he began to speak the truth and to denounce them, so they threatened him. Therefore he would not enter the city except when they were heedless.

﴿He found in it two men fighting: this one is of his faction﴾, that is, of those who supported him in his religion from the Children of Israel. It was said that he was al-Samiri. The *shīʿah* (faction) of a man are his followers and helpers. ﴿And this one is of his enemy﴾, that is, of his opponents from the Copts, and he was Fatun. It was said that for both of them one says *hādhā, wa-hādhā* (this, and this), even though they were absent, by way of narration. That is, when the observer looks at them, he says, "This is of his faction, and this is of his enemy."

﴿So the one of his faction sought his help﴾, that is, asked him for support, ﴿against the one of his enemy. So Musa struck him﴾, that is, hit him with the *jumʿ kaffihi* (the gathered palm) or with the tips of his fingers, ﴿and dispatched him﴾, that is, killed him. ﴿He said: This﴾ refers to the killing that occurred without intent, ﴿is of the work of Satan﴾. He considered the killing of the disbeliever to be from the work of Satan and called it wronging himself and sought forgiveness for it. This was because the man was a *mustaʾmin* (one under protection) among them, and it is not permissible to kill a disbelieving non-combatant under protection. Or it was because he killed him before he had been permitted to kill. It is related from Ibn Jurayj: it is not for a prophet to kill what he has not been commanded to kill. ﴿Indeed he is a manifest enemy, misleading﴾, that is, clearly hostile.

"He said, 'My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me,'" (﴿قالَ رَبِّ﴾) — O my Lord — ﴿إنِّي ظَلَمْتُ نَفْسِي﴾ "I have wronged myself" through an act that became a killing — ﴿فاغْفِرْ لِي﴾ "so forgive me" my slip — ﴿فَغَفَرَ لَهُ﴾ "so He forgave him" his slip — ﴿إنَّهُ هو الغَفُورُ﴾ "indeed He is the Forgiving" by pardoning the lapse — ﴿الرَحِيمُ﴾ "the Merciful" by removing the shame.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 17:

﴿He said, "My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me, I will never be a supporter (ẓahīran, helper) of the criminals (al-mujrimīn)."﴾ "Supporter" (ẓahīran) means one who gives aid (mu'īnan). "The criminals" (lil-mujrimīn) means the disbelievers (lil-kāfirīn).

"By what You have bestowed upon me" (bi-mā an'amta 'alayya) is an oath (qasam) whose answer (jawāb) is omitted (maḥdhūf), its implied meaning being: "I swear by Your favour upon me, [namely] the forgiveness, that I will certainly repent, so I will never be a supporter of the criminals." By "backing the criminals" he meant accompanying Pharaoh, being incorporated into his company, and increasing his numbers, since he used to ride with his riding, like a child with a parent.

﴿So he became in the city, fearful,﴾ for his own sake, lest he be seized for his killing of the Copt, ﴿watching out﴾ (a circumstantial clause, ḥāl), meaning: anticipating the help of his Lord. In this is evidence that there is no harm in fearing other than God, contrary to what some people say, that fear of other than God is not permissible. ﴿Then behold, the one﴾ — "idhā" here is for sudden surprise (lil-mufājaʾah), and what follows it is the subject (mubtadaʾ) — ﴿who had sought his help﴾, namely Moses, ﴿yesterday, was crying out to him﴾, seeking aid (yastaghīthuhu). The meaning: the Israelite whom Moses had rescued sought his help a second time against another Copt.

﴿Moses said to him﴾, namely to the Israelite, ﴿Indeed, you are clearly misguided﴾, meaning: astray from right guidance, manifestly in error. For you fought a man yesterday and killed him on your account. The one who is rightly guided in his management does not do an act that leads to calamity for himself and for the one whom he wants to help.

﴿So when he wished to strike the one who﴾ Musa ﴿wished to strike﴾ the one who, namely the Qibti (the Egyptian), ﴿who is an enemy to both of them﴾, to Musa and to the Israelite, because he was not of their religion, or because the Copts were enemies of the Children of Israel. ﴿He said﴾ the Israelite to Musa, peace be upon him, and he suspected that Musa intended to seize him, not the Qibti, since he said to him: ﴿"Indeed you are clearly a person who causes trouble."﴾ ﴿"O Musa, do you intend to kill me as you killed a person"﴾, meaning the Qibti, ﴿"yesterday? You only want"﴾ what you want ﴿"to be a tyrant"﴾, that is, one who kills in anger, ﴿"in the land"﴾, the land of Egypt, ﴿"and you do not want to be among the reformers"﴾ in restraining anger. The killing of the Qibti the day before had become widely known, but its killer had remained unidentified. When he disclosed it concerning Musa, peace be upon him, (p-٦٣٥) the Qibti learned that its killer was Musa, so he informed Pharaoh, and they resolved to kill him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 20:

﴿And a man came from the farthest part of the city﴾ He was the believer of Pharaoh's family (Mu'min Al Fir'awn), and he was a cousin of Pharaoh. ﴿Running﴾ is an adjective (sifah) of "a man," or a circumstantial clause (hal) from "a man," because he was described by the phrase "from the farthest part of the city." ﴿He said: O Musa, indeed the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you﴾ That is, some of them are instructing one another to kill you, or they are consulting together concerning you. Al-i'timar (conspiring, taking counsel) means consultation; it is said: "The two men yatatamaran and ya'tamiran," because each of them instructs his companion regarding something or advises him on a matter. ﴿So leave﴾ the city. ﴿Indeed I am to you among the sincere advisers.﴾ The phrase "lak" (to you) is a clarifying complement (bayan) and is not a complement (silah) of "al-nasihin" (the sincere advisers), because a silah may not precede the mawsul (the element it completes). It is as if he had said: "Indeed I am among the sincere advisers," then he wished to clarify, so he said "lak," as it is said: "saqyan laka" (watering to you) and "marhaban laka" (welcome to you).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 21:

﴿So he went out﴾ Musa, ﴿from it﴾, from the city, ﴿in fear, watching warily﴾, expecting to be confronted on the road or to be pursued by someone who would kill him. ﴿He said: "My Lord, deliver me from the wrongdoing people"﴾, i.e., the people of Pharaoh.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 22:

﴿When he turned towards Madyan﴾ — i.e., towards it. Al-tawajjuh (turning towards) means directing oneself toward something. Madyan (Madyan) is the town of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him. It was named after Madyan ibn Ibrahim. It was not under the authority of Pharaoh, and the distance between it and Egypt was eight days' journey. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "He set out without knowing the way, relying only on good opinion of his Lord." ﴿He said: "It may be that my Lord will guide me to the right path."﴾ That is: its middle and the bulk of its course. Then an angel came to him and set off with him toward Madyan.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 23:

﴿And when he arrived﴾ (reached) ﴿the water of Madyan﴾, their water from which they gave drink, and it was a well. ﴿He found upon it﴾, upon the side of the well, ﴿a community﴾, a group ﴿of people﴾, of people of differing kinds, ﴿watering﴾ their livestock. ﴿And he found, besides them﴾, in a place lower than their place, ﴿two women holding back﴾, driving away their sheep from the water, because those who were on the water were stronger than them, so they could not gain access to watering, or lest their sheep mix with their sheep. Al-dawd is driving away and repelling. ﴿He said: "What is your matter?"﴾, what is your affair. Its real sense is "what is your makhtub (object of concern)", i.e., what is your objective in holding back, so the object of concern was called khatb. ﴿They said: "We do not water"﴾ our sheep ﴿until the shepherds depart﴾ with their livestock. "Yasdura" is read by Ibn 'Amir (Shami), Yazid and Abu 'Amr, meaning: return. Al-ri'a' is the plural of ra'in, like qa'im and qiyam. ﴿"And our father is an old man"﴾ who cannot water the sheep ﴿"great"﴾ in his condition, or in age, unable to tend the sheep. They presented their excuse to him for taking charge of the watering themselves.

﴿So he watered [their flock] for them﴾: he watered their sheep for their sake, out of a desire for good and to relieve the distressed. It is narrated that he moved the people away from the mouth of the well and asked them for a bucket. They gave him their bucket and said, "Draw water with it." It was a bucket that only forty men could lift, yet he drew water with it alone, poured it into the trough, and invoked blessing.

The object is omitted in "yasquna" (they water [their flocks]), "tadhuddan" (they hold back [their flocks]), "lā nasqī" (we do not water [our flocks]), and "fasaqā" (he watered), because the purpose is the act itself, not the object of the act. Do you not see that he took pity on them? That was because they were occupied with holding back [their flocks], while the others were occupied with watering, and he did not pity them merely because their flock was sheep and the flock being watered was camels, for example. Likewise in "lā nasqī" and "fasaqā," the intended thing is the watering, not the one watered.

The correspondence between their answer and his question is this: he asked them about the reason for holding back [their flocks], and they said, "The reason is that we are two women, modest and weak. We cannot compete with men, and we are ashamed to mix with them. So we must delay watering until they have finished."

Shuʿayb, peace be upon him, approved of his two daughters watering livestock, because this matter in itself is not forbidden and religion does not reject it. As for manliness (murūʾah), the customs of people regarding it differ. The circumstances of the Arabs in this respect differ from those of the non-Arabs, and the way of the people of the desert differs from the way of the people of settled towns, especially when the situation is one of necessity.

﴿Then he turned back to the shade﴾: that is, the shade of an acacia tree (samurah). In this is evidence that resting in this world is permissible, contrary to what some of the ascetics (mutaqashshifa) claim. When the trial grew long upon him, he found comfort in complaint, for there is no fault in complaining to the Master. ﴿So he said, "My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever (good) You have sent down to me, in need"﴾: that is, for whatever (good), whether little or much, plain or rich. "Faqīr" means needy, and it is followed by the preposition "li" (for) because it is treated as implying "seeking" or "requesting." It is said that he had not tasted food for seven days, his belly clinging to his back. It may also be understood as: "I am in need of this world for the sake of the good of religion You have sent down to me, which is salvation from the wrongdoing people," because he had been with Pharaoh in dominion and wealth. He said this out of contentment with the good recompense, joy in it, and gratitude for it.

Ibn ʿAṭāʾ said: he looked from servanthood (ʿubūdiyyah) to lordship (rubūbiyyah), and he spoke in the language of need because of the lights that had come upon his inner secret.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 25:

﴿Then one of the two women came to him, walking shyly. She said: "Indeed my father invites you, so that he may reward you for watering [our flocks] for us."﴾ "Shyly" (ʿalā istiḥyāʾ) is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), meaning: bashfully. This is evidence of her complete faith and the nobility of her lineage, for she was inviting him to her home and did not know whether he would accept, so she came to him bashfully, having covered herself with the sleeve of her garment. The "mā" in "mā saqayta" is a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah), meaning: as a reward for your watering.

It is related that when the two of them returned to their father earlier than the other people, and their flocks were full-uddered, he said to them: "What has made you hasten?" They said: "We found a righteous man who had mercy on us and watered for us." He said to one of them: "Go and call him to me." Then Musa (ʿalayhi al-salam) followed her, and the wind pressed her garment against her body, and she described him [to her father]. He said to her: "Walk behind me and direct me to the way."

﴿So when he came to him and related to him the narrative﴾: that is, his story and his circumstances with Pharaoh. "Al-qaṣaṣ" is a verbal noun used to refer to the thing narrated. ﴿He said﴾ to him: ﴿"Do not fear. You have escaped from the wrongdoing people."﴾ For Pharaoh had no authority in our land. In this is evidence for the permissibility of acting on the report of a single transmitter, even if he is a slave or a woman. Walking with a non-related woman is, nevertheless, [to be avoided] with caution and scrupulousness. As for taking a wage for good and charitable deeds, it is said that there is no harm in it when there is need, as was the case for Musa (ʿalayhi al-salam). Yet it is related that when she said "so that he may reward you," he disliked that, and he only accepted so as not to disappoint her intention, for the one who intends has a sanctity. When Shuʿayb placed the food before (p-638) him, he refrained, and Shuʿayb said: "Are you not hungry?" He said: "Yes, but I fear that it may be a recompense for what I watered for them. We are a household that does not sell its religion for worldly gain, nor take a price for a kindness." Then Shuʿayb (ʿalayhi al-salam) said: "This is our custom with everyone who comes to stay with us," and he ate.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on Surah 28, verse 26:**

﴿One of the two women said, "O my father, hire him. Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy."﴾ Take him as a hired worker to tend the sheep. It is narrated that the elder of the two was called Safra' and the younger was called Sufayra'. Safra' is the one who took him away and asked her father to hire him, and she is the one he married. ﴿Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy.﴾ He said, "What makes you know of his strength and trustworthiness?" She mentioned his drawing up the bucket and her instruction to walk behind him. The verb is given in the past tense, "اسْتَأْجَرْتَ" (istajarta), to indicate that his trustworthiness and strength are two established matters. Her statement, ﴿Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy,﴾ is a comprehensive saying, because when these two qualities, capability and trustworthiness, are combined in the one who handles your affairs, your mind is relieved and your purpose is accomplished. It was also said: "strong" in his religion and "trustworthy" in his limbs. By this saying, which has become like a proverb, she was spared from having to say, "Hire him for his strength and trustworthiness."

It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) that the three most perceptive of people are: the daughter of Shu'ayb; the companion of Yusuf in his saying ﴿Perhaps he will benefit us﴾ [Yusuf: 21]; and Abu Bakr concerning Umar.

﴿He said, "Indeed, I want to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine"﴾: I want to give you one of them in marriage (uzawwijaka). His saying "these two" (hatayn) indicates that he had other daughters. This was a promise (mu'wada) from him, not a marriage contract (aqd nikah), for had it been a contract he would have said, "I have married you [to her]." ﴿On condition that you serve me﴾: that you be a hired worker (ajir) for me, from ajartuhu, when you are his hired worker. ﴿For eight years﴾: this is an adverbial of time (zarf). A hijjah is a year, and its plural is hijaj. Marrying on condition of tending sheep is permissible by consensus (ijma'), because it falls within the category of fulfilling the duties of marriage, so there is no contradiction, unlike marrying on condition of service (khidmah). ﴿And if you complete ten﴾: that is, the work of ten years. ﴿Then it is from you﴾: that is an act of grace (tafaddul) from you, not an obligation upon you. Or it means: its completion is from you, and I do not make it obligatory upon you; but if you do it, it is from you (p. 639) an act of grace and voluntary kindness. ﴿And I do not want to burden you﴾: by imposing upon you the completion of the longer of the two terms. The real meaning of their saying "shaqaqtu 'alayhi" and "shaqqa 'alayhi al-amr" (the matter burdened him) is that when a matter becomes great for you, it is as if it has burdened you; your thinking of it in two ways: sometimes you say, "I can bear it," and at other times, "I cannot bear it." ﴿You will find me, if God wills, among the righteous﴾: in good dealing and in fulfilling the covenant. It is also permissible that righteousness be meant in its general sense, which includes good dealing. His conditioning it on God's will regarding the righteousness he promised signifies reliance upon God's enabling him in it and His help, for if God wills, he does it, and if He does not will, he does not do it.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on Surah 28, verse 28:**

﴿He said﴾ Moses. ﴿That﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), and it refers to what Shu'ayb had made a covenant with him about. The predicate (khabar) is ﴿between me and you﴾. That is: what you have said, and what you covenanted me upon and stipulated with me, stands between us both entirely. Neither of us will depart from it. Neither I, regarding what you imposed on me, nor you, regarding what you imposed on yourself.

Then he said ﴿whichever of the two terms I fulfil﴾. That is: whichever term of the two I fulfil, meaning ten years or eight. The word ﴿أيّ﴾ (ayyu, "whichever") is in the accusative, governed by ﴿قَضَيْتُ﴾ (qadaytu, "I fulfil"). The word ﴿ما﴾ (ma) is superfluous (za'ida) and emphatic (mu'akkida), to strengthen the indefiniteness of ﴿أيّ﴾. The construction is conditional (shartiyya), and its answer (jawab) is ﴿there shall be no transgression against me﴾. That is: no aggression shall be made against me in demanding more than it.

Al-Mubarrad said: He knew that there would be no transgression against him in either of the two terms. But he combined them so that the lesser would be treated as the fuller in fulfilment. Just as demanding more beyond the fuller term is transgression, so demanding more beyond the lesser term is also transgression.

﴿And God is Witness over what we say﴾. The word ﴿وكيل﴾ (wakil, "Guardian/Trustee") is derived from ﴿وَكَلَ إليه الأمر﴾ (to entrust a matter to someone), and it is transitive with ﴿على﴾ (ʿalā), because it has been used in the sense of "witness" and "watcher" (raqib).

It is related that Shu'ayb had the staffs of the prophets, peace be upon them. He said to Moses at night: "Enter that house and take a staff from those staffs." So he took a staff which Adam had brought down from Paradise. The prophets, peace be upon them, had continued to inherit it until it came to Shu'ayb. He touched it, and he was blind, so he was reluctant to part with it. He said: "Take another." But nothing came into his hand except it, seven times. So he knew that it had a station.

When morning came, Shu'ayb said to him: "When you reach the fork of the road, do not take the path to your right, for although the pasture there is more abundant, there is in it a serpent (tinnin) which I fear for you and for the flock." So the flock took the path to the right, and he was unable to restrain them. He followed their trail, and he found grass and abundance the like of which he had never seen. He slept, and behold, the serpent had approached. The staff fought against it until it killed it, and then returned to Moses' side, bleeding. When he saw it bleeding and the serpent slain, he was gladdened by that.

When he returned to Shu'ayb, he touched the flock and found them full-bellied and abundant in milk. Moses informed him, and he rejoiced and knew that Moses and the staff had a station. He said to him: "I have given you, from the offspring of my flock this year, every speckled and spotted (adra' wa-dar'a) animal." Then it was revealed to him in a dream: "Strike your staff upon the watering-place of the flock." He did so, and then he watered them. All of them gave birth to speckled and spotted young, and so he fulfilled his condition to him.

(p-640)

﴿When Musa had fulfilled the term﴾. He, upon him be peace, said: He fulfilled the more complete of the two terms and married the younger of the two daughters. This is contrary to the narration that has passed. ﴿And he set out with his family﴾, with his wife, toward Egypt. Ibn 'Ata' said: When he had completed the term of the trial (al-mihna, a period of testing) and the days of nearness (al-zulfa, closeness to God) drew near, and the lights of prophethood appeared, he set out with his family so that they might share with him in the subtle gifts of his Lord's making. ﴿He perceived a fire from the side of the Mount. He said to his family, "Stay here; indeed I have perceived a fire. Perhaps I will bring you from it some news"﴾ about the road, because he had lost his way. ﴿Or a burning brand from the fire, that you may warm yourselves﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 30:

﴿So when he came to it, he was called from the right-hand side of the valley﴾ relative to Musa, ﴿in the blessed place﴾ by Allah the Exalted speaking to him therein, ﴿from the tree﴾ — the ʿunnāb (jujube) or the ʿawsaj (hawthorn) — ﴿that: "O Musa"﴾. The particle ʿan (that) is either explanatory (mufassira) or the light form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy (thaqīla) ʿanna. ﴿Indeed, I am Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾.

Jaʿfar said: he saw a fire, which guided him to the lights, because he saw the light in the form of fire. When he drew near to it, the lights of holiness enveloped him and the robes of intimacy surrounded him. He was addressed with the gentlest address and was asked for the best response, and thereby he became a noble interlocutor. He was given what he asked for and was secured from what he feared.

"Al-jadhwa" (a burning brand, a firebrand) — it is read in three dialects, and it has been recited with all three: ʿĀṣim read the jīm with a fatḥa, Ḥamza and Khalaf read it with a ḍamma, (p-641) and the others read it with a kasra. It means a thick stick, whether or not there was fire at its tip.

The first "min" (from) and the second are for the beginning of the limit (ibtidāʾ al-ghāya), meaning: the call came to him from the side of the valley, from the direction of the tree. And "min al-shajara" (from the tree) is a substitute (badal) for "min shāṭi' al-wādī" (from the side of the valley), a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimāl), because the tree was growing on the shore, i.e., the side.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 31:

﴿And throw down your staff﴾. It was said to him, "Throw down your staff," so he threw it, and Allah turned it into a serpent (thu'ban). ﴿When he saw it moving﴾ (tahtazz), meaning it was moving (tataharrak), ﴿as if it were a snake (jann)﴾, meaning a snake (hayyah) in its quick gliding, though it was a serpent (thu'ban) in its body. ﴿He turned and fled without looking back﴾, meaning he did not return. Then it was said to him, ﴿"O Musa, come forward and do not fear. Indeed you are among the secure"﴾, meaning: you are safe from anything harmful reaching you from the serpent.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 32:**

﴿Sluk﴾ (insert): ﴿put your hand into your bosom﴾, meaning the opening of your shirt, ﴿and it will come out white﴾, having a radiance like the radiance of the sun, ﴿without harm﴾, meaning leprosy. ﴿And draw your wing to you against fear﴾. The Hijazi reader recites "al-rahb" with two fathas, and the Basri reader too. Hafs recites "al-rahb" and the others recite "al-ruhb". The meaning of all of them is fear. The meaning is: draw your hand to your chest, and what you feel of fright will go away, that is, for the sake of the serpent. From Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, every frightened person who places his hand on his chest, his fear departs. It has also been said that the meaning of drawing in the wing is that when Allah the Exalted turned the staff into a serpent, Musa was startled and warded it off with his hand, as a frightened person does with something. He was told: your warding it off with your hand carries disgrace before the enemies. So when you throw it down and it turns into a serpent, put your hand under your armpit in place of warding it off with it, then bring it out white, so that both aims are achieved: avoiding what is a disgrace to you, and displaying another miracle. The "wing" here means the hand, because a person's hands are in the position of a bird's two wings. When he puts his right hand under his left armpit, he has drawn his wing to himself. Or the drawing of the wing to himself may mean steadying himself and controlling his self when the staff turns into a serpent, so that he does not tremble or become afraid. This is a metaphor (istiʿara) drawn from the behavior of a bird, for when a bird is frightened it spreads its wings and lowers them; otherwise its wings are folded against it and gathered up. The meaning of "from the fear" is "because of the fear", that is: if fear afflicts you at the sight of the serpent, then draw your wing to yourself. He made the fear that afflicted him a cause or reason for what he was commanded regarding drawing his wing to himself. The meaning of ﴿draw your wing to you﴾ and ﴿put your hand into your bosom﴾ is one thing according to one of the two explanations, but the two expressions are varied because the aims differ: the aim of the first is the hand coming out white, and the aim of the second is the concealing of fear. The meaning in Surah Taha of "draw your hand to your wing" is: put your right hand under your left. ﴿Those two﴾, with light (takhfif), is the dual of "dhalika"; with emphasis (tashdid), it is the reading of Makki and Abu ʿAmr, the dual of "dhalika", in which one of the two nuns is a substitute for the omitted lam. What is meant is the hand and the staff. ﴿Two proofs﴾, meaning two clear, luminous arguments. The argument was called a proof (burhan) because of its luminosity, from the expression used for a fair-skinned woman: "barharhah". ﴿From your Lord to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾, meaning: We have sent you to Pharaoh and his chiefs with these two signs. ﴿Indeed they were a people who were defiantly disobedient﴾, meaning disbelieving.

He said: "My Lord, I have killed a man among them, so I fear that they will kill me."

بِهِ. وبِالياءِ يَعْقُوبُ.

"Bihi." (with it). "Wa-bil-yā'i Ya'qūb." (And Ya'qūb reads it with the yā' [ي], i.e., "yaqtulūnī," with the first-person object pronoun written as yā' after the nūn.)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 34:

﴿And my brother Harun, he is more eloquent in tongue than me, so send him with me﴾ Hafs (read) "ridan" (as a helper) as a state (hal), meaning: an aid. It is said: radat-hu, i.e., a'antuhu (I aided him). And without hamza, (it is read by) Madani.

﴿to confirm me﴾: Asim and Hamza (read it as) an attribute (sifah), meaning: a helper confirming me. The others read it in the jussive (bi-l-jazm) as an answer (jawab) to "arsilhu" (send him).

The meaning of his confirming Musa is his aiding him by adding clarification in the places of dispute (madhann al-jidal), if he needs it, so that he may establish his claim, not that he should say to him, "You have spoken the truth." Do you not see his saying: ﴿He is more eloquent in tongue than me, so send him﴾? The excellence of eloquence is only needed for establishing the proof, not for saying "you have spoken the truth"; so Sahban and Baqil are equal in this.

﴿Indeed, I fear that they will deny me﴾: "yukadhdhibuni" (they will deny me) in both states, (read by) Ya'qub.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 35:

﴿He said: "We will strengthen your arm through your brother."﴾ We will reinforce you by means of him, since the hand grows strong through the strength of the upper arm, for it is the support of the hand; and the whole body is strengthened through the strength of the hand in handling affairs. ﴿And We will give you both authority﴾ dominance, power, and awe in the hearts of the enemies. ﴿So they shall not reach you, by Our signs﴾ The bāʾ (by) is connected to yaṣilūna (they shall reach), meaning: they shall not reach you because of Our signs, and the sentence is complete. Or, [it is connected to] fa-najʿalu lakumā sulṭānan, meaning: We will empower you by Our signs. Or it is connected to a omitted element, meaning: go with Our signs. Or it is an explanation of al-ghālibūna (the victorious), not a complement. Or it is an oath whose answer is lā yaṣilūna (they shall not reach), placed before it. ﴿You two and those who follow you are the victorious.﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 36:

﴿Then when Musa came to them with Our clear signs﴾ (wāḍiḥāt, "clear"), ﴿they said, "This is nothing but fabricated magic"﴾. That is: magic that you have devised and then attributed to Allah falsely; or, magic that is described as fabricated, like all other kinds of magic, and is not a miracle from Allah. ﴿And we never heard of this among our forefathers of old.﴾ "Fī ābā'inā" (among our forefathers) is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) construction, mansūba, referring back to "hādhā" (this), meaning: existing in their time. That is: we were never told of its existence among them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 37:

﴿And Moses said, "My Lord knows best who has come with guidance from Him, and who will have the good outcome of the abode. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not prosper."﴾ That is: "My Lord knows better than you who it is whom Allah has qualified for the greatest success, in that He made him a prophet, sent him with guidance, and promised him the good final outcome" — meaning himself. And even if he were, as you claim, a lying sorcerer, He would not have qualified him for this, because He is Self-Sufficient and Wise; He does not send liars, nor does He make sorcerers prophets, and the wrongdoers do not prosper in His sight. The "good outcome of the abode" is the praiseworthy outcome, in accordance with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those, for them is the good outcome of the abode﴾ [al-Ra'd: 22], "Gardens of Eden." By "the abode" is meant the worldly life, and its outcome is that the servant is concluded with mercy and good pleasure, and the angels receive him with glad tidings and forgiveness.

"Qala Musa" (And Moses said) without a waw: Makki reads it so, and it is good, because the context is one of questioning and inquiry about what Moses answered them when they called such great signs "fabricated magic." The reasoning for the other reading (with the waw) is that they said that, and Moses said this, so that the observer may weigh one statement against the other and discern the falsehood of one and the soundness of the other. (p-644)

"Rabbi a'lamu" (My Lord knows best): read by the Hijazi reciters and Abu 'Amr. "Man yakunu" (who will have): read by Hamza and Ali.

And Pharaoh said, "O chiefs, I know of no god for you other than myself." By negating his knowledge of another god, he intended the negation of its existence, meaning: you have no god other than me. Or it is to be taken literally, and that another god is unknown to him.

﴿So kindle for me, O Haman, a fire upon the clay﴾, that is, bake for me bricks and make them. He did not say "bricks" (ājurr) because he was the first to make bricks, so he teaches him the craft by this expression. And because it is more eloquent and more befitting the speech of tyrants, since the command of Haman, who was his minister, to kindle upon the clay is addressed by calling him by name with "yā" (O) in the middle of the speech, is a sign of arrogance and tyranny.

﴿Then build for me a tower (ṣarḥ)﴾, a high palace, ﴿that I may ascend (aṭṭaliʿ)﴾, that is, I may climb up; so ṭulūʿ and iṭṭilāʿ mean ascending, ﴿to the god of Moses﴾. He supposed that He, exalted is He, is in a place just as he himself was in a place. ﴿And indeed I think he (Moses) is among the liars﴾, that is, Moses, in his claim that he has a god and that He sent him to us as a messenger. The forsaken one contradicted himself, for he said, "I know of no god for you other than myself," then he revealed his need for Haman and affirmed a god for Moses, and reported that he was not certain of Moses' lying. It is as if he sheltered himself from the staff of Moses, peace be upon him, so he obfuscated and said, "that I may ascend to the god of Moses."

It is narrated that Haman gathered fifty thousand builders and built a tower the like of which no creature had reached. Then Gabriel, peace be upon him, struck the tower with his wing and cut it into three pieces: one piece fell upon the army of Pharaoh and killed a thousand thousand men; one piece fell into the sea; and one piece fell in the west. None of his workers remained except that he perished.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 39:

﴿And he became arrogant, he and his soldiers﴾ grew great (taʿazzama) ﴿in the land﴾ the land of Egypt ﴿without right﴾ i.e., falsely. So arrogance belongs to God, may He be exalted, who is the Proud (al-Mutakabbir) in reality, meaning the one who is supremely great in the magnificence of His majesty, as our Messenger ﷺ related from his Lord: "Pride is My cloak and greatness is My garment; whoever contends with Me over either of them, I will cast him into the Fire." Every other proud person (p-645) is proud without right. ﴿And they thought that they would not be returned to Us﴾ — yarjiʿūn (they will be returned) is read by Nafiʿ, Ḥamzah, ʿAlī, Khalaf, and Yaʿqūb.

Then We seized him and his hosts, and We cast them into the sea. This is from the overwhelming discourse by which He indicated the greatness of His majesty: He likened them, in their insignificance relative to their number, even though they were a vast multitude, to pebbles which a man took up in his palm and threw into the sea. ﴿So look﴾, O Muhammad, ﴿at how was the end of the wrongdoers﴾, and warn your people, for you will be victorious over them.

[Qur'anic verse] "And We made them leaders (a'immah), calling to the Fire" — that is, to the deeds of the people of the Fire.

Ibn 'Ata' (Ibn 'Ata' al-Adami, a Sufi master) said: He has withdrawn from their inner secrets divine success (tawfiq) and the lights of realization (tahqiq), so they are in the darknesses of their souls and do not guide to the path of right guidance.

In this is evidence for the doctrine that the acts of servants are created (khalq af'al al-'ibad), [meaning God creates human actions].

[Qur'anic verse] "And on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped" — from the punishment.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 42:

﴿And We made them follow up in this world with a curse﴾ We obligated them to expulsion and removal far from mercy. It was also said: it is what befalls them of the people cursing them, by enumerating them (their sins). ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the despised﴾, the expelled, the removed far away, or the destroyed, disfigured with blackness of faces and blueness of eyes. "Yawm" (day) is an adverbial complement (zarf) for "al-maqbuhin" (the despised).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 43:

﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book﴾ the Torah, ﴿after We had destroyed the earlier generations﴾ the people of Noah, Hud, Salih and Lot, peace be upon them, ﴿as insights for mankind﴾. This is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the Book. Basira (insight) is the light of the heart by which one perceives guidance and happiness, just as baṣar (sight) is the light of the eye by which one sees. The meaning is: We gave him the Torah as lights for hearts, because they were blind, unable to gain insight, and did not distinguish truth from falsehood. ﴿And a guidance﴾ and a direction, because they were floundering in error. ﴿And a mercy﴾ for whoever follows it, because when they act upon it they attain the attainment of mercy. ﴿That they may remember﴾ that they may take admonition. (p-646)

Surah 28, verse 44 in al-Nasafi's commentary (Madarik al-Tanzil):

﴿And you were not﴾ O Muhammad ﴿on the western side﴾ of the mountain, ﴿the western side﴾ meaning the place situated on the western slope, which is where the appointed time (mīqāt) of Musa took place, ﴿when We decreed to Musa the command﴾, i.e., We spoke to him and brought him near as a confidant (najiyy). ﴿And you were not among the witnesses﴾, i.e., among those who witnessed the revelation to him, so that you could stand, by way of direct observation, on what befell Musa at his appointed time.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 45:

﴿But We produced⁠ generations⁠﴾ after Musa (Moses), ﴿and their lifetimes grew long⁠﴾. That is: their lifespans lengthened, prophethood became intermittent (fatrah), the reports were close to being lost, the sciences were effaced, and distortion (tahrif) occurred in much of them. So We sent you as a renewer (mujaddid) of those reports, clarifying what distortion had befallen them, and We gave you knowledge of the stories of the prophets and the story of Musa. It is as if He said: you were not a witness to Musa and what happened to him, but We revealed it to you. He mentioned the cause of the revelation, which is the lengthening of the interval (of prophethood), and by it indicated the effect (al-musabbab) concisely. Thus this istidrak (corrective transition) resembles the two istidrakat after it.

﴿And you were not dwelling⁠﴾ (resident, staying) ﴿among the people of Madyan⁠﴾, who are Shu'ayb and those who believed in him, ﴿reciting to them Our verses⁠﴾, reading them to them as one who learns from them; he means the verses in which is the story of Shu'ayb and his people. The word ﴿tatlu⁠﴾ (reciting) is in a position of accusative as a second predicate (khabar thani) or as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿thawiyan⁠﴾. ﴿But We were sending⁠ messengers⁠﴾: but We sent you and informed you of them and taught them to you.

﴿And you were not on the side of the Mount (Tur) when We called﴾ Musa, "Take the Book with strength." ﴿But﴾ We informed you and sent you as ﴿a mercy﴾ to the merciful ﴿from your Lord, that you may warn a people to whom no warner had come before you﴾ in the time of the fatrah (the interval between prophets) between you and Jesus, which was five hundred and fifty years, ﴿so that they may remember﴾. (p. 647)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 47:

﴿And had it not been that a calamity should befall them﴾ as a punishment ﴿for what their hands have sent forth﴾ of disbelief and wrongdoing. Since most actions are carried out by the hands, actions are attributed to the hands, even though some are actions of the heart, by giving precedence to the majority over the minority. ﴿They would say﴾ at the time of the punishment: ﴿Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger, so that we might follow Your signs and be among the believers?﴾ The first "law" (lawla) is for impossibility (imtina'iyya), and its response is omitted. The second is for urging (tahdid), and the first fa' is for coordination ('atf), while the second fa' is the response of lawla, because it has the force of a command, since a command prompts an action, and the one who prompts and the one who urges are of one kind. The fa' may enter the response of a command. The meaning is: Were it not that they would say, when they are punished for what they had sent forth of polytheism and sins, "Why did You not send to us a messenger?", arguing against Us with this, We would not have sent to them. That is, the sending of a messenger to them is only so that the proof is established against them, not so that they are compelled to accept it, as in His saying ﴿so that mankind will have no argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ [al-Nisa: 165]. If you say, how does this meaning hold, when the punishment has been made the cause of sending, not the saying, since lawla of impossibility enters upon it and not upon the saying? I say: the saying is the intended thing, in that it is the cause of sending; but since the punishment was the cause of the saying, and its existence came about with the existence of the punishment, the punishment was treated as if it were the cause of sending, so lawla was placed before it, and the saying was brought after it, conjoined by the fa' that gives the sense of causality. Its meaning returns to your saying: "And were it not for their saying this when a calamity befalls them, We would not have sent."

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 48:**

﴿So when the truth came to them from Us﴾, i.e., the Qur'an or the Messenger, confirming the Book, being miraculous, ﴿they said﴾, i.e., the disbelievers of Makkah, ﴿"Why was he not given the like of what was given to Musa?"﴾, i.e., "Why was he not given (هَلّا أُعْطِيَ, "hallā" meaning "why not"; "uniya" meaning "given") the like of what was given to Musa" ﴿of the Book sent down all at once﴾, ﴿"Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Musa before?"﴾, meaning: the sons of their own kind, those whose way is their way and whose obstinacy is their obstinacy, and they are the disbelievers in the time of Musa, peace be upon him, ﴿before the Qur'an﴾. ﴿They said﴾ about Musa and Harun: ﴿"Two sorceries that back each other up"﴾ (p-648), i.e., they support each other. "Two sorceries" (siḥrān) is the reading of al-Kufi, meaning "two possessors of sorcery," or they made them "two sorceries" as an intensification in describing them with sorcery. ﴿And they said: "Indeed we are, in each of them, disbelievers."﴾, i.e., in each one of the two. It was said that the people of Makkah, just as they disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Qur'an, had also disbelieved in Musa and the Torah, and they said about Musa and Muhammad, "Two sorcerers who back each other up," or about the Torah and the Qur'an, "Two sorceries that back each other up." This was when they sent a delegation to the leaders of the Jews in Madinah to ask them about Muhammad (ﷺ), and they informed them that he was mentioned in their Book. The delegation returned to Quraysh and informed them of the words of the Jews, and at that they said, "Two sorcerers who back each other up."

Qur'anic verse: ﴿Say: "Then bring a Book from Allah that is better guided than these two; I will follow it, if you are truthful."﴾

Commentary: "Than both of them" refers to what was revealed to Musa (Moses) and what was revealed to me (ﷺ). ﴿Atta'biuhu﴾ (I will follow it) is the answer to the imperative ﴿fa'tu﴾ (bring). ﴿In kuntum sadiqin﴾ (if you are truthful) means: in your claim that the two are sorcery (sihran).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 50:

﴿Then if they do not respond to you, know that they only follow their own desires.﴾ "Then if they do not respond to your call" to bring the Book that is more guiding (al-Kitab al-Ahda), "know that they have been left without excuse, and there remains for them no argument except following their whims (al-hawa)." ﴿And who is more astray than one who follows his own desire without guidance from Allah?﴾ That is: there is no one more astray than one who follows his desire in religion, "and without guidance" is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: forsaken, and not left free between himself and his desire. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 51:

﴿And We have indeed caused the word to reach them in succession, that they may remember.﴾ Al-Tawsil (tawsil: intensifying and repeating the joining) means making the joining abundant and repeated. The meaning is: the Qur'an came to them consecutively and continuously, with promise and warning, narratives and lessons, and admonitions, so that they might remember and thereby prosper. (p-649)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 52:

﴿Those to whom We gave the Book before it﴾ — before the Qur'an. The predicate of "those who" is ﴿they, in it﴾ — in the Qur'an — ﴿believe﴾. It was revealed concerning the believers among the People of the Book.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 53:

﴿When the Qur'an is recited to them, they say: "We believe in it. Indeed it is the truth from our Lord. Indeed, we were Muslims before it."﴾ "Before it" means before the revelation of the Qur'an, "Muslims" meaning those who were upon the religion of Islam, believers in Muhammad (ﷺ). His statement "Indeed, it is the truth" is a reason (ta'lil) for believing in it, because its being the truth from Allah makes it fitting to believe in it. His statement "Indeed, we..." is an explanation (bayan) of his statement "We believe," because it may be a faith of recent origin or of long standing, so they informed that their faith in it was long established.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 54:

﴿Those will be given their reward twice, because they were patient.﴾ Due to their patience in faith in the Torah and faith in the Qur'an; or due to their patience in faith in the Qur'an before its revelation and after its revelation; or due to their patience in bearing the harm of the polytheists and the People of the Book. ﴿And they repel evil with good﴾ they repel disobedience with obedience; or they repel harm with forbearance. ﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ they give zakat (purification).

﴿And when they hear vain talk﴾ — that is, falsehood or abuse — ﴿from the polytheists, they turn away from it and say﴾ to the frivolous ones, ﴿"To us our deeds, and to you your deeds. Peace be upon you."﴾ — that is, a pledge of safety from us to you, by which we will not return your vain talk with its like. ﴿We do not seek the ignorant﴾ — we do not want to mix with them or keep their company.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 56:

﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like﴾: you are not able to bring into Islam everyone among your people and others whom you wish to enter it. ﴿But Allah guides whom He wills﴾: He creates the act of being guided (i'tida', "being guided") in whomever He wills. ﴿And He is most knowing of those who are guided﴾: of those who choose guidance, accept it, and take heed of the proofs and signs.

Al-Zajjaj (Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj, a grammarian and exegete) said: The exegetes have unanimously agreed that it was revealed concerning Abu Talib. That was because when he was on his deathbed he said: "O assembly of Banu Hashim, affirm Muhammad and you will prosper." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O uncle, you command them to give advice to themselves, and you leave it for yourself!" He said: "What do you want, nephew?" He said: "I want you to say: There is no god but Allah; I will testify for you by it before Allah." He said: "Nephew, I know well that you are truthful, but I dislike that it be said that he faltered (khari'a) at the time of death."

Although the wording is general, the verse is a proof against the Mu'tazilah, for they say that guidance (huda) is merely clarification. "He has guided all people," yet they were not guided because of their poor choice. This shows that beyond clarification there is something called guidance, which is the creation of the act of being guided and the granting of success (tawfiq) and capability (qudrah).

And they said, "If we follow the guidance with you, we will be snatched away from our land." Have We not established for them a secure sanctuary?

Quraysh said: "We know that you are upon the truth, but we fear that if we follow you and oppose the Arabs in this, they will snatch us away from our land." So God silenced them (the idiom *fa-alqamahumu Allahu al-hajar*, literally "God fed them the stone") by [showing] that He had established them in the sanctuary, which He made secure by the sanctity of the House, and He made its inhabitants secure by its sanctity, and the fruits are brought to it from every direction, while they are disbelievers. How, then, could it be consistent for Him to expose them to being snatched away and to strip them of security when they have joined to the sanctity of the House the sanctity of Islam?

The attribution of security to the people of the sanctuary is literal (*haqiqah*), while its attribution to the sanctuary itself is metaphorical (*majaz*).

﴿Yujba ilayhi﴾ is read with the feminine *ta'* (as *tujba*) by Madani, Ya'qub and Sahl, meaning: it is brought and gathered.

﴿Thamarat kulli shay'﴾: the meaning of totality ("all") here is abundance, as in His saying: ﴿And she was given of everything﴾ [al-Naml: 23].

﴿Rizqan min ladunna﴾: it is a verbal noun (*masdar*), because the meaning of *yujba ilayhi* is "is provided with sustenance." Or it is an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-hi*). Or it is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) from *al-thamarat*, if it carries the sense of *marzuq* (provided), since it is specified by the genitive construction, just as it is put in the accusative when it is an indefinite noun (*nakirah*) specified by a qualifier.

﴿Wa-lakinna akthararahum la ya'lamun﴾: this is connected to *min ladunna*, meaning: few of them acknowledge that this provision is from God, while most of them are ignorant and do not know this. Had they known that it is from God, they would have known that fear and security are in His hand, and they would not have feared being snatched away if they believed in Him.

(p-651)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 58:

﴿And how many a town have We destroyed, which exulted in its livelihood!﴾ This is a warning to the people of Makkah of the evil end of a people who were in a situation like theirs, with Allah's bounty upon them, but they did not give thanks for the blessing and met it with exultation (buṭar), so they were destroyed. ﴿Kam⁠﻿ (how many)﻿ is in the accusative governed by ﴿ahlaknā (We destroyed)﻿, and ﴿maʿīshatahā (its livelihood)﻿ is in the accusative by the omission of the preposition and the conveying of the verb, meaning: in its livelihood. Buṭar (exultation) is the poor handling of wealth, which is that one does not preserve the right of Allah in it. ﴿So those are their dwellings﻿ — their homes, whose traces remain, which they witness on their journeys, such as the lands of Thamud, the people of Shuʿayb, and others. ﴿Have not been inhabited﻿ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the element governing it is the demonstrative (al-ishārah). ﴿After them, except a little﻿ — from habitation (al-suknā), meaning: none has dwelt in them except the traveller and the passer-by of the road, for a day or an hour. ﴿And We are the inheritors﻿ of those dwellings from their inhabitants, meaning: none has the right to dispose of them except Us.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 59:

﴿Your Lord would never destroy the cities﴾ at any time, ﴿until He had sent in their mother [city] a messenger﴾. The reading with a kasra on the hamza (إ) is that of Hamza and ʿAli, meaning: in the town which is their mother, i.e., their origin and main centre, ﴿a messenger﴾, in order to establish the proof and cut off excuse. Or: it was not in the judgement of God and His preceding decree that He would destroy the cities in the earth until He sent to the Mother of the Cities, meaning Makkah, because the earth was spread out from beneath it. ﴿a messenger﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿reciting to them Our signs﴾, i.e., the Qur'an. ﴿And We were never to destroy the cities unless their people were wrongdoers﴾, i.e., We did not destroy them as a punishment unless its people deserved the punishment through their wrongdoing, which is their persistence in disbelief, their obstinacy, and their arrogance after the proof had been made clear to them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 60:

﴿And whatever you have been given of a thing, it is the enjoyment of the worldly life and its adornment.﴾ And whatever you have attained of the means of this world, it is nothing but enjoyment and adornment, for a few days, and they are the duration of this perishing life. ﴿And what is with Allah﴾, that is His reward, ﴿is better﴾ in itself than that, ﴿and more lasting﴾, because it is everlasting. ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ that what remains is better than what perishes. Abu 'Amr (Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala') allowed the reading with the ya' (يا) and the ta' (تا) as alternatives, while the rest of the readers read it with the ta' (تاء) only, and nothing else. (p-652) From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: Allah Most High created the world and made its people three categories: the believer, the hypocrite, and the disbeliever. The believer provides for himself (for the Hereafter), the hypocrite adorns himself, and the disbeliever enjoys himself. Then he established this verse with his saying.

﴿Is then one to whom We have made a good promise, and he is to meet it,﴾ meaning Paradise. Nothing is better than it, because it is everlasting. For this reason Paradise is called al-Husna (the Best). ﴿and he is to meet it﴾ means he will see it, reach it, and attain it. ﴿is he like one whom We have given enjoyment in the life of this world, and then on the Day of Resurrection he will be among those brought forth?﴾ That is, among those who will be brought to the Fire, and the like. ﴿So they denied him, and they will indeed be brought forth﴾ [al-Saffat: 127]. It was revealed concerning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and Abu Jahl, may Allah curse him, or concerning Ali, Hamzah and Abu Jahl, or concerning the believer and the disbeliever.

As for the meaning of the first fa' (the particle fa', expressing sequence or consequence), it is that when Allah mentioned the difference between the enjoyment of the life of this world and what is with Allah, He followed it with His saying, ﴿Is then one to whom We have made a good promise...﴾, meaning: after this clear difference, does He equate the people of this world with the people of the Hereafter? The second fa' expresses causation, because meeting what has been promised is caused by the promise. The word thumma (then) expresses the lapse of time between the state of being brought forth and the state of enjoyment. As for "thumma huwa" (then he), the word huwa is written with a damma, which is the pronoun "he". It is as was said: the word ʿaḍd (the arm) is used for ʿaḍud, and the separated pronoun is treated like the attached one.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 62:

﴿And on the Day He calls to them﴾ God calls out to the disbelievers with a call of reproach. This is either coordinated with "the Day of Resurrection" (ʿaṭf), or it is in the accusative governed by "udhkur" (remember). ﴿So He will say: Where are My partners﴾ according to their assumption ﴿whom you used to claim﴾. The two objects of "tazʿumūn" (you claim) are omitted; its estimated form is: "kuntum tazʿumūnahum shurakāʾī" (you used to claim them to be My partners). It is permissible to omit the two objects in the category of ẓanantu (I thought/supposed), but it is not permissible to restrict oneself to only one of them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 63:

﴿Those against whom the Word has been justified will say﴾: that is, the devils, or the leaders of disbelief. The meaning of "the Word has been justified against them" is that what it entails became binding upon them and was established, and that is His word: ﴿Surely I shall fill Hell with jinn and men all together﴾ [al-Sajdah: 13]. ﴿Our Lord, these﴾: a subject (mubtada'). ﴿whom we led astray﴾: that is, we called them to polytheism and made error seem attractive to them; this is a qualifier (sifah), and the returning pronoun to the relative clause is omitted, and the predicate (khabar) is ﴿we led them astray﴾. The kaf in ﴿as we went astray﴾ is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), its estimated form being: "We led them astray, so they went astray with a going-astray like the going-astray we underwent." They mean: we only went astray by our own choice, and so these likewise went astray by their own choice, because our leading them astray was nothing but whispering and making things seem attractive. Thus there is no difference between our error and their error. Even though our enticement was a summons for them to disbelief, in opposition to it was God's summons to them to faith, through the proofs of reason He placed in them, the messengers He sent to them, and the books He sent down upon them. This is like His saying: ﴿And Satan will say when the matter has been decided: Indeed, God promised you the promise of truth﴾ [Ibrahim: 22], up to His saying: ﴿so blame yourselves﴾ [Ibrahim: 22]. ﴿We disavow to You﴾: from them, and from what they chose of disbelief. ﴿They did not used to worship us﴾: rather, they worshipped their desires and obeyed their appetites. The omission of the conjunction (al-'atf) from the two sentences is because they both affirm the meaning of the first sentence.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 64:

﴿And it will be said﴾ to the polytheists: ﴿Call upon your partners﴾, that is, the idols, so that they may deliver you from the punishment. ﴿So they will call upon them, but they will not respond to them﴾, meaning they will not answer them. ﴿And they will see the punishment. If only they had been guided!﴾ The answer to "law" (if only) is omitted, meaning: "when they saw the punishment."

﴿And mention the day when He calls out to them and says, "What answer did you give to the messengers?"﴾ [the messengers] who were sent to you. He first described what rebukes them for taking partners (shurakā') along with Him. Then [he described] what the devils say, and they are the ones who led them astray. Then [he described] what resembles gloating over them, because of their calling on their gods for help and those gods' inability to aid them. Then [he described] what they are silenced with, namely the argument made against them through the sending of messengers and the removal of every excuse.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 66:

﴿Then the news became obscure to them on that Day﴾ The proofs (ḥujaj) or the reports (akhbar) were hidden from them. It is also said: the answer was hidden from them, so they did not know what to answer with, since they had no answer. ﴿So they will not question one another﴾: they do not ask one another for an excuse or a proof, in hope that one of them has an excuse or a proof, because they are equal in their inability to answer.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 67:

﴿Then as for one who repents﴾ from polytheism ﴿and believes﴾ in his Lord and in what came from Him ﴿and does righteous deeds, it may be that he will be among the successful﴾. That is: it may be that he will be successful with Allah. The word "it may be" (ʿasā) from the Generous (al-Karim) is a certainty (taḥqīq). In it there is good news for the Muslims of Islam and an encouragement for the disbelievers toward faith. It was revealed as a response to the statement of al-Walid ibn al-Mughira: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two cities?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31]. He meant either himself or Abu Mas'ud.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on Surah 28, verse 68:

﴿And your Lord creates whatever He wills﴾. In this is evidence for the creation of acts (*khalq al-af'al*, the doctrine that God creates human actions). It is to be paused at ﴿وَيَخْتارُ﴾ (*wa-yakhtar*, "and chooses"), meaning: "Your Lord creates whatever He wills, and your Lord chooses whatever He wills." ﴿It is not for them to choose﴾, meaning: it is not for them to choose anything over God, and the choice belongs to Him over them. He did not introduce the coordinating particle (*al-'atif*, the conjunction) into ﴿ما كانَ لَهُمُ الخِيَرَةُ﴾ (*ma kana lahumu al-khiyara*, "it is not for them to choose"), because it is an explanation (*bayan*, an explanatory apposition) of His words ﴿وَيَخْتارُ﴾, since the meaning is: the choice belongs to God, and He is the most knowing of the wisdom in His acts. So none of His creatures may choose over Him. Whoever connects it so that the meaning is "and He chooses what they have a choice in" has gone far astray. Rather, ﴿ما﴾ (*ma*, here a negative particle) negates the choice of creatures, implicitly affirming the choice of the Truth. Whoever says that its meaning is "He chooses for the servants what is better and more beneficial for them" inclines toward Mu'tazilism (*al-i'tizal*, the Mu'tazila school). The word *al-khiyara* derives from *al-takhayyur* (choosing) and is used both in the sense of the verbal noun, meaning the act of choosing, and in the sense of the chosen one, as in the saying: "Muhammad is God's chosen one (*khiyaratu Allah*) from among His creation."

﴿Glory be to God, and exalted is He above what they associate with Him﴾, meaning: God is free of their association, and He is exalted above anyone having any choice over Him.

Your Lord knows what their breasts conceal (تُكِنُّ, i.e., tukinnu: they hide, keep secret) of enmity toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and envy of him, and what they disclose (مِن مَطاعِنِهِمْ فِيهِ, i.e., their criticisms of him, and their saying: "Why was someone else not chosen over him for prophethood?").

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 70:**
